Research and software

Start with a noisy read.

Insertions and deletions shift a read out of alignment. BCJRFormer uses a sliding window and a Transformer to infer what was transmitted. The PyTorch model supplied the operation order, tensor shapes, and trained parameters for the hardware implementation.

SystemVerilog testbench

Clock the RTL.
Check every output.

The testbench resets the core, sends each parameter word and waits for its acknowledgment, then sends the frame. The checker reads the RTL output port and compares each signed integer with the Python result at the same position. It checks output order, the final-output flag, and successful completion.

Read the code in execution order

How the simulation works.

The converter prepares the numbers on disk. The SystemVerilog testbench drives those numbers into the core one clock edge at a time. The checker compares the core’s outputs with answers computed in Python. Follow three real values from frame 00 below.

Pack weightsBuild the frameDrive the RTLCheck the outputs

1. Convert the trained weights and assign addresses

The saved PyTorch export contains named tensors. The converter maps each PyTorch name to the corresponding RTL tensor name and verifies its shape and scalar order. It scales each number by 1024, rounds to nearest with ties to even, and clamps it to the signed 16-bit range.

Follow the first parameter. PyTorch’s to_patch_embedding.0.weight[0] is about 0.990295231. It maps to embedding.norm_f.gamma[0]. After scaling and rounding, it becomes 1014. The manifest puts this tensor first, so the first line of parameters.hex is 03f6, the hex encoding of 1014. The first line corresponds to word address 0.

See the conversion and packing code 
# convert_bcjrformer_bundle.py · quantize()
raw = round(value * 1024)
return max(-32768, min(32767, raw)), not -32768 <= raw <= 32767

# parameter_manifest.py · write one 16-bit hex word per line
args.image.write_text(''.join(f'{v&65535:04x}\n' for v in image),encoding='ascii')

The converter calls the manifest script with the quantized tensor JSON. The manifest script concatenates the tensors in RTL address order. The completed file contains 687,991 words.

Converter, lines 29, 59 and 118–141 · Manifest writer, lines 23 and 66–76

2. Prepare the frame and compute the answer key

The converter selects sample 0 from the software capture and sorts its tokens in input order. Software has already turned the noisy read into a sliding-window representation. The frame has 144 positions and 27 features per position. The flattened array places all 27 features of position 0 first, then all 27 for position 1, and so on.

Follow one input feature. At position 0, feature 13 (zero-based) is approximately 0.025 in the capture. It becomes 26 after scaling and rounding, so line 14 of features.txt is 26. The frame also has 144 padding bits, all zero. Zero means the position is valid.

See how Python calculates the expected words 
# convert_bcjrformer_bundle.py
result = Reference(shape, parameters, features, mask).run()

The integer reference runs the decoder using the packed weights, the quantized feature words, and the mask. The runner extracts the resulting expected_f10 column into expected.txt. The first line is -680. The saved floating-point PyTorch logit for that position, -0.66001004, is used for the separate software comparison.

Frame selection and Python call, lines 90–105 and 148–165 · Integer decoder, line 62 · Text vector export, lines 33–38

3. Compile the design and load it through the host interface

The simulator reads testbench/files.f in dependency order. It starts at trained_frame_tb, which instantiates core_sim_top with the trained dimensions. That wrapper connects the flat testbench signals to the actual decoder core. The +vectors=... argument identifies the folder containing the four input files.

The testbench parses the files into arrays, checks the number and range of their entries, and resets the core. On each parameter transfer it presents an address and value, asserts param_valid, and waits for a rising edge with param_ready high. The core controller sends a write request to the parameter bank. After the memory responds, the core raises param_rsp_valid and the testbench checks param_rsp_error before sending the next word.

Follow address 0 into parameter memory 
param_addr = addr_t'(i);
param_data = act_t'(params[i]);
param_valid = 1;
do @(posedge clk); while (param_ready !== 1'b1);
@(negedge clk);
param_valid = 0;
do @(posedge clk); while (param_rsp_valid !== 1'b1);
if (param_rsp_error !== 1'b0) $fatal(1, "Parameter write failed at %0d", i);

For i = 0, this sends 03f6 to address 0. Inside the RTL, the memory adapter performs the actual write to words[index]. After all acknowledgments, the testbench pulses parameter_commit. The controller checks that the full image was loaded before enabling frame acceptance. The testbench then sends 3,888 feature words and 144 mask bits, waiting for the relevant ready signal and marking the last item in each stream.

Testbench, lines 26 and 55–108 · Controller, lines 143–170 · Memory write, line 64

4. Compare each logit and print PASS

On a rising clock edge with logit_valid high, the testbench checks the output index and the last-output flag. It reads logit_data as a signed integer and compares it with the corresponding element of expected[]. The core receives parameter, feature, and mask signals. The expected array stays in the testbench.

Follow output position 0. The checker reads -680 from the simulated RTL port and -680 from line 1 of expected.txt. It repeats that comparison for all 144 positions. The case inequality operator !== also treats an unknown RTL value as a mismatch.

See the comparison and the PASS condition 
actual = int'(logit_data);
if (actual !== expected[outputs]) begin
  $error("Output %0d expected %0d, got %0d", outputs, expected[outputs], actual);
  mismatches++;
end
outputs++;

When completion_valid arrives, the testbench requires successful completion, clear protocol and numeric error flags, exactly 144 outputs, and zero mismatches. Any failed condition calls $fatal before the display statement.

$display("PASS: %0d/%0d exact matches, status=%b, cycle=%0d",
         outputs, N, status, cycles);
$finish;

For each of the ten lab runs this printed PASS: 144/144 exact matches, status=0001, cycle=1533280239. The low status bit records rounding during inference.

Ten captured frames.

All ten frames passed with 1,440 of 1,440 exact integer output matches against fixed-point Python. Frame 00 passed in Xcelium and frames 01–09 passed in VCS. Each frame uses the same checkpoint and contains one unpadded read.

00010203040506070809

Software comparison

1,431 of 1,440 decoded bits agree

All 1,440 RTL checks passed. The nine disagreements came from comparing decoded bits between fixed-point Python and floating-point PyTorch. A decoded bit is 1 when the logit is zero or positive, and 0 when it is negative.

All nine PyTorch logits were slightly negative. After quantizing the inputs and weights and using fixed-point arithmetic throughout inference, the corresponding logits were slightly positive. Small numerical changes near zero can flip a bit. The final values show where each sign changed. Tracing intermediate values would show which operation contributed most.

Frame 01, position 129. PyTorch produced approximately −0.026463, which gives bit 0. Fixed-point Python produced the raw word 19, which represents 19 / 1024 = 0.0185546875 and gives bit 1. The VCS testbench expected the RTL to output exactly 19, and frame 01 passed all 144 comparisons.

Against the saved target bits at these nine positions, fixed-point Python was correct five times and PyTorch was correct four times.

Small-core synthesis and backend

The backend used F=2, M=2, N=2, D=2, H=1, K=2. The ten-frame RTL simulation used the full trained configuration.

Synthesis and layout

Design Compiler mapped the small core to Tower FS120 standard cells at a 200 ns trial period. At the typical corner it reported +0.05 ns setup slack, +0.32 ns hold slack, and 1,052,431.25 total cell area in library units. The writable weight memory used standard cells.

Innovus placed the core, connected the VDD/VSS rings and rails, fixed 142 signal pins, and built a clock tree with 8,801 sinks. The six-metal layout was routed, repaired for antenna violations, and filled. With the corrected propagated clock, slow-corner setup at 200 ns failed with −67.570 ns worst slack, so the lab target was revised to 300 ns.

Post-route results at 300 ns

  • Slow setup at 1.65 V and 125 °C had +27.961 ns worst slack and zero failing paths.
  • Fast hold at 2.017 V and −40 °C had +0.141 ns worst slack and zero failing paths.
  • Electrical checks reported zero violations after upsizing one NOR and three inverters and rerouting. All four max-transition violations cleared.
  • Innovus physical checks found zero geometry and antenna violations and no signal or supply connectivity problems.

The refilled core was exported as bcjrformer_dc_top.gds with the matching bcjrformer_dc_top_lvs.v. Tower foundry-deck DRC and extracted LVS remain pending. The full trained configuration still needs its own backend implementation.

Backend measurements and checkpoints

Project milestones

The full trained configuration passed the ten-frame RTL comparison. The small core completed synthesis, routing, and post-ECO timing checks at 300 ns.

How weights and signals move through the chip

Weights arrive through the parameter input pins and go into writable memory. The core reads those weights while it processes frames. To replace the weights, the host waits for the core to become idle, sends the complete new set from address zero, and sends parameter_commit. New weights must fit the same model dimensions.

A signal pin is a connection point on the edge of the block. For example, the feature_data[0] pin is on the south edge. Signal routing draws the metal path from that pin to the cells that use it. Power wiring connects the cells to VDD and VSS. The clock tree carries clk to the registers so it arrives at roughly the same time.

We’re keeping the writable memory described in the RTL. The small synthesis run built it from Tower FS120 standard cells and reported zero memory macros. The lab instructor confirmed that a previous lab design used synthesizable memory and passed DRC and LVS. Foundry-deck DRC and LVS remain pending for BCJRFormer.
